newsitem.title: USA: U.S. stocks seen lower at opening, eye on bonds.
newsitem.headline: U.S. stocks seen lower at opening, eye on bonds.

text.p: Wall Street stocks are expected to open lower after Tuesday's late rout which saw the Dow Industrials shed an earlier 100-point gain and close lower.
As was the case yesterday, bonds are seen again leading stocks and analysts said that Tuesday's volatility was indication of the situation which this high-valuation market is in.

"The Dow is at a level where you could have volatility like this every day," said Larry Wachtel, analyst at Prudential Securities. "Blue chips have been driven up by index-fund buying which is out of alignment with reality."
He said the Dow Industrials now had to move lower to the levels of the broad market.
"Swings of 100 points will become an average occurrence. This is no longer a placid Dow," Wachtel said.
Investors will be watching the December durable goods data due at 0830 EST/1330 GMT which is expected to show an increase of 1.2 percent compared to 1.6 percent decline in November.
"If the data are stronger than expected we will see further pressure on the bond market," said Peter Cardillo, director of research at Westfalia Investments.

He said that markets are likely to have a tough time moving higher with the long bond yield nearing seven percent. He said a drop of a further two to three percent in the Dow Industrials was possible.
"This market is still not finished correcting. Yesterday's reversal showed that," Cardillo said.
In Tokyo, the Nikkei Average was up 538.73 points, or 3.03 percent at 18335.30.
In London, The FTSE 100 Index was off 34.7 at 4202.7.

Among U.S. shares traded in London, International Business Machines Corp was up 1/4 at 151. Intel Corp was up 1/4 at 151-1/4 and Compaq Computer Corp added 1/8 at 84-5/8. Warner-Lambert Co was up 1/2 at 72-3/4.
The dollar soared against the yen in Tokyo and was just off its session lows against the mark in Europe.
U.S. Treasuries were weak, with the long bond down 14/32 to yield 6.96 percent.

The Wall Street Journal's Heard on the Street writes that paper makers have been reporting dismal fourth quarter results. Some warn that product prices are likely to remain depressed through the first quarter. Even so, many analysts think the industry is nearing the bottom of a slump that began in late 1995.

The New York Times Market Place writes that the U.S. Treasury will begin auctioning $7 billion in 10-year inflation-indexed bonds that will likely pay an interest rate of a little more than 3.5 percent.
